analysis.one_liner: Taxes handguns, assault weapons, and ammo to pay hospitals for treating gunshot victims.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Bill Bradley in January 1994, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal manufacturer's tax on handguns by 20 percent and on semiautomatic assault weapons and their ammunition by 19 percent, added a 30 percent tax on retail sales and transfers of these guns, and raised the three-year federal gun dealer license fee to $3,000 [S2][S3]. The money would have gone into a new Gun Violence Trauma Care Trust Fund, which would pay grants to hospitals and trauma centers stuck with unpaid bills for treating gunshot victims [S2][S3]. The bill's findings note that public funds already cover more than 80 percent of hospitalization costs for firearm injuries, roughly $3 billion a year in health care costs [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals and trauma centers that treat large numbers of gunshot victims without being paid would receive federal grants, and taxpayers would stop footing the bulk of those costs through existing public health spending [S3]. Communities with high rates of gun violence, whose local hospitals absorb the uncompensated care, would benefit most [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals and taxpayers bearing gunshot-care costs

how_it_helps.text: Creates a trust fund that grants federal money to not-for-profit hospitals, trauma centers, and other providers that incurred substantial uncompensated costs treating gunshot victims [S3].

The bill's findings state public funds pay over 80 percent of hospitalization costs for firearms injuries and that health care costs of firearm injuries run about $3 billion a year, so the taxes would shift part of that burden from taxpayers to gun purchases [S3].

Raises the federal firearms dealer license fee from roughly the existing low fee to $3,000 for three years, ending what the bill calls a taxpayer subsidy to the licensing system, which ATF put at more than $28 million a year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of handguns, semiautomatic assault weapons, and their ammunition would pay a 30 percent retail tax plus higher manufacturer taxes built into prices, and the roughly 280,000 licensed gun dealers would pay $3,000 every three years instead of the current fee [S2][S3]. Gun manufacturers and dealers would bear reduced demand as prices rose [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun and assault-weapon buyers and dealers

drawbacks.text: The taxes would fall on all buyers of the covered firearms, including low-income owners, and a 30 percent retail tax on top of a 20 percent manufacturer tax would raise the price of a handgun substantially [S3].
The money raised would cover only a fraction of the problem: the bill itself estimates firearm injury health costs at about $3 billion a year, and gun tax revenue would offset only part of that [S3].

Critics of gun taxation generally argue such measures price out lawful sport shooters while doing little by itself to stop violence, since the bill raises money for treatment rather than restricting access; the bill's own text exempts sporting firearms from the higher taxes in recognition of this concern [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift a real, documented cost — hospital care for gunshot victims that taxpayers currently cover — onto the products that generate it, while modestly raising prices for buyers and fees for dealers. It is a funding mechanism, not a violence-prevention measure, and the revenue would cover only part of the estimated $3 billion annual cost. The tradeoff is narrow: a meaningful new funding stream for trauma centers versus higher costs concentrated on purchasers of handguns, assault weapons, and ammunition [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the 103rd Congress ended without any vote or hearing.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Bradley introduced the bill on January 25, 1994, and spoke about it on the Senate floor [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the only committee action recorded [S5].
No cosponsors signed on, no further committee action was recorded, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995, with the bill never reported out or voted on [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and buyers were spared the new taxes and fees, while hospitals treating gunshot victims continued to absorb uncompensated costs paid largely by public funds [S3][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun industry and buyers; hospitals left paying

for.name: Sen. Bill Bradley
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled, and the bill died there [S5].

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun industry groups
against.role: Firearms trade and gun-owner advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed gun and ammunition tax increases in the 1994 policy debate, contributing to an environment in which no senator joined the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split never got a chance to show itself; the sponsor was a Democrat [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 20 percent manufacturer tax on handguns, 19 percent on assault weapons and their ammo, a 30 percent retail sales tax, and a $3,000 dealer license fee [S2][S3]. The industry avoided all of these when the bill died in committee [S5].

The bill would have paid grants to not-for-profit hospitals and trauma centers with substantial unpaid costs from treating gunshot victims [S3]. They continued to absorb those costs after the bill died [S3][S5].
Public funds pay over 80 percent of hospitalization costs for firearm injuries, about $3 billion a year, a burden the bill would have partially shifted to gun purchases [S3].
